name: Hollowfield Cycle Workshop

do: Name the part and the measurement
Say what a job will not fix
Describe the work, not the rider
dont: Never mention lifestyle, freedom, or the ride of your life
Never quote or imply a price before the bike has been seen
Never call a job quick, easy, or painless
Never describe a bike as beautiful, admired, or a work of art
Never use racing or marketing jargon such as marginal gains, game-changing, or revolutionary
Never promise a turnaround the workshop has not stated
Never claim to be the best or the only workshop of its kind

offerings.name: Winter Service Plan
features: Chain wear measured and reported each visit
offerings.description: A quarterly strip-down through the salt season: drivetrain cleaned and measured, cables replaced, brakes bled, bearings checked.

offerings.name: Hand-Built Wheelset
features: Rim and hub chosen with the rider
Tension chart supplied with the build
One free re-true after the first month
offerings.description: A pair of wheels laced and tensioned by hand on our own bench, built to the rider's weight and the roads they ride.

positioning: For commuters and audax riders whose one bike carries real winter mileage, Hollowfield is the arch where two mechanics work a bench each and quote every job in writing first — because a three-week wait that returns your bike with the same worn drivetrain on it was never a service.

composition_plan.intent: First row of the specification split: the narrow column labels what this place is and where it stands, the wide column states the work and offers one way to start it. Nothing centred, nothing softened.
One large statement of the workshop's method beside a narrow column of detail, so conviction and specifics sit on the same row rather than in separate sections.
One idea per full-width row — bench capacity, quoting before work, measurement and reporting — so each commitment can be read on its own and none blur together.
The sequence a bike actually goes through, sequential and ordered by the list itself, so the customer knows where the written quote falls in the order of events.
A held rail of capability labels while the detail of the work scrolls past it, letting the reader stay oriented in a dense body of technical detail.
The offerings side by side, one column each, with what is and is not included given the same weight so the boundaries are read, not discovered later.
A band of figures the business has already stated, each under a short label, to anchor the claims in verifiable facts rather than adjectives.
Open and close the awkward questions — exclusions, waits, what a job will not fix — where a prospective customer expects to find them.
Address, email and telephone alone, so someone who has decided can act without scrolling back through the page.
